title: Sable and the Tide
premise: Rafael Thornbury has spent ten years writing anonymous letters to a stranger named Sable — his only outlet for grief over his late wife and the guilt he carries about the night she died. When a new neighbor, Wren Sable, moves in next door, Rafael discovers she is the recipient of every letter: his late wife arranged the correspondence before her death as a lifeline for them both. As their friendship deepens into love, Rafael must confront that his wife orchestrated this second chance — and that forgiving himself, not her, is the real obstacle. When the bookshop faces closure and Wren learns he knew her identity weeks before telling her, Rafael must choose between protecting his secret and fighting for a love that demands total honesty; he confesses everything, loses her briefly, and wins her back by publishing their letters as a book that saves both the shop and them.
about_author: Bram Iversen is the pen name of a former coastal bookseller who spent fifteen years recommending novels to strangers before writing one of his own. He lives in a rented flat above a shuttered post office, where he still answers every letter he receives by hand.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Opening on a rain-soaked October morning, Rafael runs his failing bookshop, tends his eight-year-old daughter June, and mails his 120th anonymous letter to a stranger named Sable. The beat is weary routine hiding grief; readers sense the letters are his confession booth.

chapters.title: A Moving Van at Number Nine
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren Sable arrives next door, fleeing a failed engagement and a career she abandoned. She unpacks boxes of letters she's kept for a decade — correspondence from an unknown writer who somehow knows her heart. The beat is cautious hope: she moved here chasing the letters' return address.

chapters.title: Borrowed Umbrellas
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm forces an awkward first meeting under Rafael's awning; June immediately adopts Wren. Rafael feels an inexplicable pull he resents. The beat is reluctant chemistry — two guarded people pretending to be casual neighbors.

chapters.title: What the Dead Arrange
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Sorting his late wife Elena's belongings, Rafael finds her hospice journal revealing she secretly chose 'Sable' from a support group and gave Wren his return address before dying. He is shattered: his most private ritual was his wife's design. Beat: betrayal braided with awe.

chapters.title: The Reading Corner
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren starts volunteering at the shop, reading to June. She quotes lines from her mysterious correspondent without knowing she's quoting Rafael to his face. He recognizes his own words in her mouth. Beat: vertigo — intimacy built on concealment.

chapters.title: Salt and Second Chances
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A beach walk with Wren cracks open his loneliness; he nearly tells her about the letters and doesn't. Meanwhile the shop's landlord, developer Marcus Hale, serves notice of rent doubling. Beat: rising stakes on two fronts — love and livelihood.

chapters.title: June's Map
chapters.summary: June's POV (childlike third person). June, missing her mother, draws a map of 'people who belong together' placing Rafael and Wren side by side. Rafael finds it and panics at how visible his heart has become. Beat: tender dread — a child sees what adults deny.

chapters.title: Hale's Offer
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Marcus offers to save the shop if Rafael sells him the building's back lot — land Elena's family left him. Accepting means betraying Elena's memory; refusing means losing everything. Beat: power's corruption introduced as a seductive, reasonable-sounding deal.

chapters.title: Letters, Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At a town literary night, Wren reads one of her anonymous letters publicly; the room weeps, and Rafael watches his own secret grief become communal art. Wren declares she'll find her writer someday. Beat: the trap tightening — his words are now famous.

chapters.title: The Almost
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. After the festival, wine and proximity lead to a near-kiss interrupted by June's nightmare. Rafael retreats, terrified of replacing Elena. Wren reads the retreat as rejection. Beat: first real rupture, self-inflicted.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rafael's oldest friend Dev discovers the truth about the letters and urges him to tell Wren, calling the silence 'a kindness that curdles.' Rafael signs Hale's preliminary agreement instead, choosing control over honesty. Beat: moral compromise compounding.

chapters.title: Sable in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts her own ghosts — she once abandoned a friend to protect her reputation, and the letters' forgiveness is why she survived. She realizes she loves Rafael but won't build on half-truths. Beat: she resolves to demand full honesty, mirroring his arc.

chapters.title: One Hundred Twenty-One
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rafael writes letter 121 addressed honestly, planning to give it to Wren — then hides it in a drawer when June asks if Wren will 'be her new mum.' Beat: fear dressed up as protection; the letter becomes a ticking object.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren learns Hale plans to demolish the shop block and that Rafael signed away the lot quietly. Feeling betrayed twice over — by the deal and the secrecy — she withdraws from the shop and from him. Beat: public stakes ignite private wounds.

chapters.title: Elena's Last Instruction
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In Elena's journal's final pages, Rafael finds explicit instruction: 'Give him to Sable whole, or not at all. He will want to hand over a curated version.' He understands his wife foresaw exactly this failure. Beat: devastating clarity; the theme lands.

chapters.title: Confession in the Stacks
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Rafael tells Wren everything in the empty shop — the letters, Elena's design, his weeks of knowing. Wren's fury is not about the deception but that he decided what she could handle. She leaves. Beat: climax of emotional conflict; love against duty.

chapters.title: The Town Rallies
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. With the auction days away, June, Dev, and townsfolk organize a protest and fundraiser using Wren's public reading of the letters as its heart. Rafael refuses to attend, believing he's forfeited the right. Beat: community as consequence and chorus.

chapters.title: Letter 121, Delivered
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. June slips Rafael's hidden letter 121 under Wren's door. It contains not excuses but the raw draft of his guilt about the night Elena died — the truth behind ten years of letters. Wren finally understands the man, not just the lie. Beat: turning point through vulnerability.

chapters.title: The Night She Died
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Full flashback: the argument, the drive, the accident, the decade of self-imposed exile. Rafael forgives the person in the mirror at last, standing in Elena's garden at dawn. Beat: internal climax — the forgiveness the blurb promised.

chapters.title: Against the Gavel
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the auction, Rafael publicly retracts the sale, exposing Hale's forged easement documents with Dev's help. Wren arrives mid-chaos; they fight for the shop and each other in front of the whole town. Beat: external climax — love and truth defeating corrupt power.

chapters.title: Signed, Finally
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Weeks later: the shop saved as a community co-op, Rafael signs his name to a new letter for the first time — no anonymity, no armor. Wren answers it by knocking on his door instead of writing back. Beat: quiet joy; duty and desire reconciled.

chapters.title: Sable and the Tide
chapters.summary: Epilogue, alternating POV. One year on: their co-authored book of letters sits in the shop window beside June's map, now framed. On the beach, the three of them write a single letter to Elena and let the tide take it. Beat: resolution — grief honored, love chosen, truth kept.
